A. Does recent evidence support the size of effect we assume: does this measure raise the share of lung cancer patients who get curative-intent treatment, and by how much?
Measure: Precise radiotherapy (SBRT) for early cancer in patients who cannot be operated. Every stage I patient who is too frail for surgery is referred for stereotactic radiotherapy (3-8 visits, no anaesthesia) instead of being left without treatment. The treatment exists in every university hospital; what is missing in some counties is the referral rule.
effect_summary_en: In a Dutch national registry study, the share of elderly stage I patients left untreated fell by 7 percentage points once SABR was available; the study did not measure the share of all lung cancer patients.
supported_en: A Netherlands Cancer Registry study (Annals of Oncology 2012) found 7% fewer elderly stage I patients left untreated after SABR became available.
not_supported_en: The pages do not show the 0.8-point gain across all patients, or any effect in Finland.
in_use_quote: Paikallisessa tai paikallisesti edenneessä taudissa, jos leikkaushoito ei ole mahdollista, voidaan antaa täsmäsädehoitoa tai yhtä aikaa säde- ja solunsalpaajahoitoa eli kemosädehoitoa.
missing_en: No page shows a rule that every inoperable stage I patient is referred for stereotactic radiotherapy, or any check that this happens.
summary_en: B: The OYS lung cancer care-pathway page says the university hospital runs the multidisciplinary lung cancer meetings and gives surgery and radiotherapy, and that patients with local disease who cannot be operated may receive targeted radiotherapy ("täsmäsädehoito"). No page shows a rule that every inoperable stage I patient is referred. A: A Dutch national registry study found a 7% absolute drop in untreated elderly stage I patients after SABR became available, which roughly supports the direction of our assumption but not its size across all patients.
unanswered_en: I found no page from Lapland's wellbeing services county (Lapha) on lung cancer radiotherapy referrals, and no Finnish data on how many inoperable stage I patients go untreated.
